new.title: Stand at the Deutsches Eck where Rhine meets Moselle
new.desc: The Deutsches Eck is the promontory where the Moselle flows into the Rhine, named after a commandery of the Teutonic Order. A monumental equestrian statue of Kaiser Wilhelm I was dedicated here in 1897, taken down after the Second World War, and a replica was later raised on the surviving plinth.
new.tip: Go early or at sunset when the two rivers show different colours and the fortress glows across the water. The riverside promenade is free.

new.title: Explore Ehrenbreitstein Fortress high above the Rhine
new.desc: Ehrenbreitstein stands on the east bank opposite the mouth of the Moselle. The Prussians built the present fortress between 1817 and 1828 on the site of an earlier one destroyed by the French, and it was never attacked. It is part of the Upper Middle Rhine Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site.
new.tip: Walk the ramparts for the best view of the confluence. Arrive by cable car and walk down for the full experience.

new.title: Ride the Rhine cable car up to the fortress
new.desc: The Koblenz cable car, also called the Rheinseilbahn, is a gondola lift that opened in 2010 for the Bundesgartenschau held the following year. It carries you across the Rhine and up to Ehrenbreitstein Fortress in a few minutes, with the Deutsches Eck spread out below.
new.tip: Pick a clear day for the view and walk back down if you like.

new.title: Step inside the Basilica of St. Kastor
new.desc: St. Kastor is the oldest surviving church in Koblenz. The first building was finished in the first half of the 9th century and today's look dates from the 12th and 19th centuries. It stands just behind the Deutsches Eck on the tip of land between Rhine and Moselle and is a key Romanesque church of the Middle Rhine.
new.tip: Pair it with a stroll to the nearby Deutsches Eck. Entry is free and the interior is quiet and cool.

new.title: Climb to Liebfrauenkirche on the highest point of the old town
new.desc: The Church of Our Lady stands at the highest point of the Koblenz old town, and its origins go back to the 5th century. Together with St. Kastor and St. Florin it shapes the old town skyline, and from the late Middle Ages until the French Revolution it was the main parish church.
new.tip: Free to enter, and a short walk from Am Plan.

new.title: Meet the Schängel fountain in the town hall courtyard
new.desc: Schängel is the local nickname for children born in Koblenz, and the city is often called the Schängel city. A fountain built for them in 1941 in the courtyard of the town hall, a former Jesuit college, became one of the city symbols.
new.tip: The courtyard is in the town hall complex, so visit during the day.

new.title: Admire the Electoral Palace and its Rhine gardens
new.desc: The Electoral Palace was built in the late 18th century for Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, the last Archbishop and Elector of Trier. It is one of the most important examples of early French neoclassical architecture in south-western Germany and later housed the Prussian crown prince, the future Wilhelm I.
new.tip: The palace is mainly federal offices inside, so enjoy the long facade from the garden side and then continue through the Rhine gardens.

new.title: Find the medieval Alte Burg by the Balduin bridge
new.desc: The Alte Burg is a former electoral castle from the 13th century standing on the bank of the Moselle beside the Balduinbrücke. Only the main residence survives and today it houses the city archive.
new.tip: Walk around the exterior and the small riverside lane. It is a quiet corner of the old town.

new.title: Visit St. Florin, the old collegiate church
new.desc: The Florinskirche is a Protestant church in the old town, built around 1100. It belonged to the St. Florin canons' foundation, which was secularised in 1802, and since 1820 it has served the Protestant congregation.
new.tip: Its Florinsmarkt square is a lively spot for a break afterwards. The building is next to the Weinhaus Hubertus.

new.title: Marvel at the neo-Romanesque Herz-Jesu-Kirche
new.desc: The Herz-Jesu-Kirche was built between 1900 and 1903 as part of the southern city extension and counts among the most important neo-Romanesque churches in Germany. The Löhr shopping centre sits just north of it.
new.tip: Step in for a quiet moment away from the shopping streets of the Löhrstraße.

new.title: Browse modern art at the Ludwig Museum
new.desc: The Ludwig Museum shows modern and contemporary art in the historic Deutschherrenhaus beside the Deutsches Eck. It was opened in 1992 and is the fifth collection started by the collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig in Germany; its first exhibition was titled Atelier de France.
new.tip: Make it a rainy day stop; the building itself is a worthwhile Teutonic Order house.

new.title: Tour the Mittelrhein-Museum in Forum Confluentes
new.desc: The Mittelrhein-Museum is the city art museum of Koblenz, founded in 1835 at about the same time as the Wallraf-Richartz Museum in Cologne and the Städel in Frankfurt. It moved into the modern Forum Confluentes on Zentralplatz in 2013 after ten relocations.
new.tip: The Forum also houses the tourist information, so combine it with a city orientation.

new.title: Cross the Balduin bridge, the oldest in Koblenz
new.desc: The Balduinbrücke is a stone arch bridge over the Moselle built in the 14th century. It is the oldest surviving bridge in the city and the last one over the Moselle before it joins the Rhine, linking the old town with Lützel.
new.tip: Stroll across at dusk, then continue along the Moselle promenade.

new.title: Walk around the Prussian Fort Konstantin
new.desc: Fort Grand Duke Konstantin was finished in 1827 and 1828 as an outer work of the Prussian fortress of Koblenz on the Karthause. It secured the heights south-west of the city and is largely preserved and protected as a monument.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk around the Karthause district.
new.q: Fort Konstantin, Am Fort Konstantin, Koblenz

new.title: Discover Fort Asterstein on the Rhine heights
new.desc: Fort Asterstein was part of the Prussian Koblenz fortress and of the Pfaffendorfer Höhe system. Built in the 1820s and partly razed in the 1920s, its central reduit survives and gave the district its name.
new.tip: It is a short walk from the fortress area and good for a quieter view of the Rhine valley.

new.title: Visit the birthplace of Beethoven's mother
new.desc: The Mutter-Beethoven-Haus in Ehrenbreitstein is the 17th-century birthplace of Maria Magdalena Keverich, mother of the composer Ludwig van Beethoven. It has been a small museum since 1975 in the old centre of Ehrenbreitstein.
new.tip: Check its opening days before you go, as small museums keep limited hours.

new.title: Stand at the Rittersturz memorial in the city forest
new.desc: The Rittersturz monument stands in the Koblenz Stadtwald and recalls the 1948 Rittersturz conference, where the western German state premiers discussed the future of western Germany.
new.tip: Combine it with a forest walk above the city.

new.title: Spot the baroque Bürresheimer Hof on Florinsmarkt
new.desc: The Bürresheimer Hof is a former noble courtyard in the old town, built in 1659 and 1660 after plans by the Capuchin friar Bonitius from Linz. Its main house now stands on Florinsmarkt.
new.tip: It is a good stop on a Florinsmarkt walk between the Hubertus wine house and the Liebfrauenkirche.

new.title: Find the Alte Münze, the old electoral mint master's house
new.desc: The Alte Münze is the former mint master's house of the electoral mint in Koblenz. The other mint buildings were pulled down, and the open space around it is now the Münzplatz in the old town.
new.tip: Check the square for a peaceful bench with a view of the old facades.

new.title: Trace Deinhard's sparkling wine roots at Deinhardplatz
new.desc: Deinhard grew from a wine merchant business opened in Koblenz in 1794 by Johann Friedrich Deinhard, and sparkling wine production began in 1843. The company is now based in Bernkastel-Kues, but its birthplace square in Koblenz still carries the name.
new.tip: This is a short history stop. For a taste of regional wine go to the nearby Altstadt wine houses.

new.title: Stroll the Rhine gardens from Deutsches Eck
new.desc: The Rheinanlagen are a 3.5 km park and promenade along the left bank of the Rhine. The older section, the Kaiserin-Augusta-Anlagen, was laid out between 1856 and 1861 by Peter Joseph Lenné as an English landscape garden for Princess Augusta.
new.tip: Walk from the Deutsches Eck upstream to the Weindorf and cross the Pfaffendorfer Brücke on the way back. Free all day.

new.title: Walk the Moselle promenade to the Deutsches Eck
new.desc: The Peter-Altmeier-Ufer runs along the Moselle through the old town, passing the Balduin bridge and the Mosellum before it ends at the Deutsches Eck. You see the Moselle bridges, the old customs buildings and pleasure boats on the water.
new.tip: Start at the Mosellum and walk toward the confluence, stopping for a drink at the Königsbacher Biergarten.

new.title: Watch the fish ladder at the Mosellum
new.desc: The Mosellum is a visitor centre at the Koblenz lock and weir that combines a modernised fish pass with an exhibition on the Moselle. Over four floors it explains water ecology, fish migration, shipping and electricity generation.
new.tip: Look through the viewing windows at the fish pass. A good rainy day option for families.

new.title: Explore the Landesmuseum inside Ehrenbreitstein Fortress
new.desc: The Ehrenbreitstein Fortress Cultural Centre houses the Koblenz State Museum, with exhibitions about the region's history and technology inside the Prussian fortress itself.
new.tip: Combine it with the fortress visit and plan a couple of hours for the exhibitions.

new.title: Learn about river life at the Rhein-Museum
new.desc: The Rhein-Museum Koblenz, founded in 1912, is a cultural history museum about life on the Rhine, with focus areas including shipping, ecology, hydrology, Rhine romanticism, tourism, economy and history.
new.tip: Good for a rainy afternoon in Ehrenbreitstein.

new.title: See historic locomotives at the DB Museum
new.desc: The DB Museum Koblenz opened in 2001 as the first outstation of the Nuremberg transport museum. It is run by volunteers and its focus is on historic locomotives of the German railways.
new.tip: It is aimed at rail fans, so check the opening days before you go.

new.title: Cross the Pfaffendorfer Brücke on foot
new.desc: The Pfaffendorfer Brücke is the oldest bridge over the Rhine in Koblenz. A first rail bridge opened here in 1864, and the present road bridge dates from 1953 after war damage. It links the city centre with Pfaffendorf and Ehrenbreitstein.
new.tip: Walk over for a postcard view of the old town and the Rhine, then return via the Rhine gardens.

new.title: Find the surviving bridge houses of the old Schiffbrücke
new.desc: A pontoon bridge crossed the Rhine between Koblenz and Ehrenbreitstein from 1819 until it was destroyed in 1945. The two bridge houses and the bridgehead on the left bank still survive in the Rhine gardens.
new.tip: Look for the two small houses by the promenade. A short detour on any Rhine walk.

new.title: Taste Moselle and Rhine wine at the Koblenz Weindorf
new.desc: The Weindorf Koblenz is a village-style wine restaurant in the Rhine gardens near the Pfaffendorfer Brücke, built in 1925 for the German wine exhibition. The menu includes regional dishes such as a Rhenish Döppekooche with apple compote, and the Traubenträger fountain figure stands in the grounds.
new.tip: Go on a warm evening to sit outside among the half-timbered houses. Try the Döppekooche.

new.title: Drink Rhine and Moselle wine in Weinhaus Hubertus
new.desc: Weinhaus Hubertus sits in a half-timbered house from 1689 on Florinsmarkt and specialises in wines from the Rhine and Moselle, by the glass or bottle.
new.tip: Order a glass of local Riesling. Arrive early evening for a seat in the old house.

new.title: Order Koblenzer Saumagen at the Winninger Weinstuben
new.desc: The Winninger Weinstuben in a stone building on the Rheinzollstraße, just steps from the Deutsches Eck, serve local specialities such as Koblenzer Saumagen along with regional wine.
new.tip: A good lunch stop after the Deutsches Eck and St. Kastor.

new.title: Share Italian plates and wine at Cofone Weinbar
new.desc: Cofone Weinbar on the Löhrstraße is an Italian restaurant with the feel of a wine bar, with a stylish and cozy room and reasonably priced wines according to guests.
new.tip: Book ahead for an evening table and ask for an Italian wine recommendation.

new.title: Eat hearty Rhenish food at Wirtshaus Alt Coblenz
new.desc: Wirtshaus Alt Coblenz stands on Am Plan, a square once used as market, tournament and event ground. The rustic tavern serves hearty regional German food and regional wines.
new.tip: Order a regional dish and enjoy the old town atmosphere on the square outside.
new.q: Wirtshaus Alt Coblenz, Am Plan 13, Koblenz

new.title: Have a late drink at Mephisto in the old town
new.desc: Mephisto is a bar on the Eltzerhofstraße in the old town that appears among the best rated bars near the Deutsches Eck.
new.tip: Go in the evening when the old town streets fill up.

new.title: Raise a beer at the Königsbacher Biergarten by the Deutsches Eck
new.desc: The Königsbacher Biergarten am Deutschen Eck sits by the Rhine promenade with a view of Ehrenbreitstein Fortress, the Deutsches Eck and the river, close to the old town.
new.tip: Aim for a late afternoon table on a clear day to watch the boats and the fortress light up.
new.q: Königsbacher Biergarten am Deutschen Eck, Koblenz

new.title: Dine on the Rhine bank at Deutschie
new.desc: Restaurant Deutschie, in an old brewery building on Am Ufer in Neuendorf, serves German and modern German dishes. Reviewers highlight the Rhine location and a beer garden.
new.tip: A good option away from the busiest old town streets. Check the evening opening hours.

new.title: Cool down with Italian gelato at Eiscafé Brustolon
new.desc: Eiscafé Brustolon on the Bahnhofplatz serves Italian ice cream made on site and a wide range of coffee specialities.
new.tip: A scoop on the way to or from the station makes a sweet start or end.

new.title: Tour the Marksburg, the Rhine castle that was never destroyed
new.desc: The Marksburg above Braubach is one of the main sites of the Rhine Gorge UNESCO World Heritage Site. Of the 40 hill castles between Bingen and Koblenz it is one of only two that were never destroyed, and the only one that never fell into disrepair, with a striking butter-churn shaped keep.
new.tip: Allow time for the uphill walk from Braubach and check tour times.

new.title: Look down from the Loreley rock
new.desc: The Loreley is a 132 m high slate rock at Sankt Goarshausen, at the deepest and narrowest part of the Middle Rhine. It towers over the river bend and looks across to Burg Katz.
new.tip: The plateau is reached by road or the Rhine ferry and trail. Come in the afternoon for the best light on the river.

new.title: Explore the huge Rheinfels castle ruins above St. Goar
new.desc: Rheinfels was started in 1245 by Count Diether V of Katzenelnbogen and became the largest fortress in the Middle Rhine valley. French revolutionary troops slighted it in 1797, but the ruins and a museum remain above the Rhine.
new.tip: Plan a couple of hours and check the museum inside.

new.title: Spot Burg Katz from the St. Goar waterfront
new.desc: Burg Katz above Sankt Goarshausen was first built around 1371 by Count William II of Katzenelnbogen. It was bombarded in 1806 by Napoleon and rebuilt between 1896 and 1898. It is privately owned and not open to visitors.
new.tip: View it from the riverside in St. Goar or from the ferry, rather than expecting to enter.

new.title: Visit the Hostile Brothers castles above Kamp-Bornhofen
new.desc: Burg Sterrenberg and Burg Liebenstein stand side by side on a steep slate ridge above Kamp-Bornhofen and are known as the Hostile Brothers. The Bornhofen monastery, an old pilgrimage site, sits beneath them.
new.tip: Walk up from the village to Sterrenberg for the views. Look for the monastery church on the way.

new.title: Climb to Burg Lahneck at the mouth of the Lahn
new.desc: Burg Lahneck is a spur castle built in the first half of the 13th century on a 164 m rock above the Lahn mouth, opposite Stolzenfels Castle. Its symmetrical oblong plan is typical of late Hohenstaufen castles, and its pentagonal keep is rare.
new.tip: Allow a steady uphill walk from Lahnstein. The castle restaurant offers a terrace.

new.title: Peek at Schloss Martinsburg in Lahnstein
new.desc: Schloss Martinsburg was built in 1298 as a toll castle by the archbishops of Mainz. It is one of the few unscathed castles on the Middle Rhine, now privately owned, and houses a carnival museum and a mint.
new.tip: Check the opening times of the museum before visiting.

new.title: Tour neo-Gothic Schloss Stolzenfels
new.desc: Stolzenfels was a ruined 13th-century castle given in 1823 to the Prussian crown prince Frederick William, who rebuilt it as a Gothic Revival palace. It is part of the Upper Middle Rhine Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site.
new.tip: Check the opening days before the uphill walk.

new.title: See the Königsstuhl where German kings were chosen
new.desc: The Königsstuhl at Rhens is an octagonal two-storey stone structure shaped like a throne. In the Middle Ages the prince-electors negotiated and chose several kings here, and the Kurverein of Rhense of 1338 strengthened their power.
new.tip: It stands on the edge of Rhens, close to the Rhine and easy to combine with a stroll in the old town.

new.title: Ride the Boppard chairlift to the Vierseenblick
new.desc: The Vierseenblick is a 273 m viewpoint above Boppard overlooking the Rhine loop. A 915 m double chairlift from 1954 lifts you 232 m in about 20 minutes. Just below the top, Gedeonseck has an inn with a panorama terrace.
new.tip: Ride up, have a coffee on the terrace and walk down through the Bopparder Hamm vineyards.

new.title: Climb to the Reichsburg above Cochem
new.desc: The Reichsburg is the landmark of Cochem, a hilltop castle at 154 m above the town. It served as a toll castle in the Middle Ages, was probably built around 1100 or in the first half of the 12th century, and was destroyed in the 17th century before it was rebuilt.
new.tip: Climb up from the town below and check the tour times.

new.title: Walk through the forest to Burg Eltz
new.desc: Burg Eltz is a medieval castle on a 70 m rock spur above the Elzbach. It has been in the hands of the Eltz family since the 12th century and, with Bürresheim and Lissingen, is one of only three Eifel castles never destroyed.
new.tip: Plan extra time for the walk to the castle through the forest.

new.title: Climb to the Burg Metternich ruin above Beilstein
new.desc: Burg Metternich is the ruin of a spur castle at 150 m above Beilstein on a rock spur about 60 m high. The village below is known for its tight lanes and Moselle views.
new.tip: Walk up from the village for the view.

new.title: Explore the twin-keep ruins of Burg Thurant
new.desc: Burg Thurant above Alken on the Moselle was a double castle. From the mid-13th century the archbishops of Cologne and Trier co-owned it, and each half had its own keep, residential buildings and entrance. It gradually fell into disrepair from the early 16th century.
new.tip: Allow time for the walk up from the village.

new.title: Find the Romanesque Matthiaskapelle at Kobern
new.desc: The Matthiaskapelle is a Romanesque central-plan chapel on the Oberburg at Kobern-Gondorf, set on a rise above the Moselle.
new.tip: Allow time for the walk up from the village.

new.title: Visit the Romanesque abbey of Maria Laach
new.desc: The Benedictine abbey of Maria Laach stands on the south-western shore of the Laacher See in the Eifel. It was built in the 11th and 12th centuries and has carried the name Maria since 1862. The monastery also runs a garden centre, book shop and other crafts.
new.tip: Visit the church, browse the monastery shops, and finish with a lake walk.

new.title: Descend into the lava cellars at the Lava-Dome in Mendig
new.desc: The Lava-Dome, German Volcano Museum, opened in 2005 in Mendig and presents the volcanism of the Laacher See region. The old lava cellars below are cold and damp at about 8 degrees, so a jacket helps.
new.tip: Book a guided cellar tour and bring a warm layer.

new.title: Look at the Alter Krahnen, Andernach's Renaissance crane
new.desc: The Alter Krahnen in Andernach is a 16th-century harbour crane built in stone beside the Rhine. It is among the few surviving Renaissance industrial monuments and is one of the city's best known sights. It was built between 1554 and 1561 and loaded millstones, tuff and wine.
new.tip: Walk the Rhine promenade past the old town wall and see it at dusk.

new.title: Climb the Golo tower at Genovevaburg in Mayen
new.desc: The Genovevaburg is the symbol of Mayen. It has been rebuilt several times since it was destroyed in 1689, and its keep is called the Golo tower after the legend of Genoveva of Brabant.
new.tip: Allow time to walk around the castle and the town of Mayen.

new.title: Tour Schloss Bürresheim near Mayen
new.desc: Schloss Bürresheim stands on rock above the Nette in the Eifel. It was never destroyed, was lived in until 1921 and is now a museum managed by the Rhineland-Palatinate heritage authority.
new.tip: Check the opening and tour times in advance.

new.title: Walk through the Ahrtor of Ahrweiler's town walls
new.desc: Ahrweiler's town fortifications date back to the mid-13th century. The moat is first recorded in 1261, the city gates in 1297 and the wall in 1298, and the whole is a protected monument.
new.tip: Stroll around the old town ring, then stop for local red wine.

new.title: Hike to the ruins of Burg Are above Altenahr
new.desc: Burg Are is the ruin of a hill castle at 240 m above Altenahr. Count Dietrich I of Are built it between 1095 and 1105, and it was first mentioned in documents in 1121.
new.tip: Follow the signed path up from the village. Best in dry weather.

new.title: Learn about the Vulkaneifel at the Vulkanmuseum Daun
new.desc: The Vulkanmuseum in the old district office of Daun is part of the Natur- und Geopark Vulkaneifel and shows photos and exhibits about the geological history of the volcanic Eifel and active volcanoes elsewhere.
new.tip: A good starting point before driving out to the nearby maar lakes.

new.title: Climb the Dronketurm for a maar view
new.desc: The Dronketurm, also called the Adolf-Dronke-Turm, is a free-standing observation tower near Schalkenmehren in the Vulkaneifel.
new.tip: Climb on a clear day for views over the maar lakes.

new.title: Admire the yellow castle of Montabaur
new.desc: Montabaur is known throughout Germany for its strikingly yellow castle on the hill and for its ICE station on the Cologne to Frankfurt line.
new.tip: Walk up from the old town to the castle.

new.title: Discover Westerwald stoneware at the Keramikmuseum
new.desc: The Keramikmuseum Westerwald in Höhr-Grenzhausen calls itself the German collection of historic and contemporary ceramics, in the heart of the Kannenbäckerland pottery district.
new.tip: Stop at the pottery workshops around town afterwards.

new.title: Stroll past the Kurhaus in the spa town of Bad Ems
new.desc: The Kurhaus in Bad Ems was built in 1715 as the Nassau bathhouse and sits in a bend of the Lahn at the heart of the spa quarter. The town is part of the UNESCO Great Spa Towns of Europe.
new.tip: Walk along the Lahn promenade and have a coffee nearby.

new.title: Climb the Concordiaturm above Bad Ems
new.desc: The Concordiaturm is a 15.1 m lookout tower built in 1861 by the local beautification society on the Bäderlei. It has two platforms and the Baedeckers Felsenweg trail passes through the grounds.
new.tip: Walk up from the spa quarter and enjoy the view of the Lahn valley.

new.title: Cross the Rhine on the Loreley ferry
new.desc: The Loreley VI ferry crosses the Rhine at river kilometre 556 and links the twin towns of St. Goar and St. Goarshausen.
new.tip: A short ride that gives views of Rheinfels, Burg Katz and the Loreley.

new.title: Race down the Loreley summer toboggan run
new.desc: The Loreley-Bob is a summer toboggan run on the plateau of the Loreley rock, inside the Upper Middle Rhine Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site.
new.tip: Good for kids and adults on a dry day.

new.title: Ride the Cochem chairlift to Pinnerkreuz
new.desc: The Cochem Sesselbahn, also called the Pinnerkreuzbahn, is a single-rope chairlift opened in 1955 and rises to the 255 m Pinnerkreuz viewpoint. From the top you can also reach the Klotten wildlife park.
new.tip: Ride up for the view over Cochem and the Moselle loop.

new.title: Cross the Moselle by Beilstein's yaw-rope ferry
new.desc: The Moselfähre Beilstein is a high-rope yaw ferry for pedestrians, cyclists and cars. It runs seasonally from Easter to the end of October between Beilstein and Ellenz-Poltersdorf, mainly for leisure traffic.
new.tip: Cross to the left bank for a view of Beilstein village and the castle ruin.

new.title: Walk around the Laacher See
new.desc: The Laacher See is a volcanic crater lake 2 km across that formed after a huge eruption around 13,000 years ago. Gas bubbles still rise at the south-eastern shore. The lake is part of the East Eifel volcanic field.
new.tip: The loop can start at the abbey.

new.title: Watch the world's highest cold-water geyser erupt
new.desc: The Andernach geyser reaches 50 to 60 m and is the highest cold-water geyser on Earth. It was first drilled in 1903 on the Namedyer Werth peninsula in the Rhine and driven by natural carbon dioxide. Eruptions last about 15 minutes with around two hours between them.
new.tip: Start at the Geysir-Zentrum on the Rhine promenade in Andernach and plan for the boat to the peninsula.

new.title: Walk around the Pulvermaar crater lake
new.desc: The Pulvermaar near Daun is almost perfectly round and 72 m deep, the deepest natural lake in Germany outside the Alps. Its area is about 38 hectares and it belongs to the Gillenfeld maars with the smaller Holzmaar.
new.tip: Walk the shore and add a stop at the nearby Holzmaar.

new.title: Visit the Nürburgring, the Green Hell
new.desc: The Nürburgring is a motorsports complex around the medieval Nürburg castle. Its Nordschleife is 20.8 km long with more than 300 m of elevation change and was nicknamed the Green Hell by Jackie Stewart.
new.tip: Check the Ring's own site for public driving sessions and visitor times.

new.title: Hike the Rotweinwanderweg from Altenahr
new.desc: The Rotweinwanderweg is a 35 km hiking trail through the Ahr valley, running from Altenahr to Bad Bodendorf through steep red wine vineyards. A suggested first stage links Altenahr to Ahrweiler.
new.tip: Start in Altenahr and stop at wine estates along the way. Check which stretches are open before you go.

new.title: Taste Bopparder Hamm Riesling at Weinhaus Heilig Grab
new.desc: Weinhaus Heilig Grab is Boppard's oldest wine tavern and has been family owned for more than 200 years. It focuses on Riesling from the Bopparder Hamm, with a cozy dining room and a garden under old chestnut trees.
new.tip: Order a 0.1 l tasting glass. Check opening days first.
new.q: Weingut Weinhaus Heilig Grab, Zelkesgasse 12, Boppard

new.title: Sip Moselle wine on the terrace of Zum Kapuziner
new.desc: Weinstube Zum Kapuziner on Pater-Martin-Straße in Cochem is a vinothek and wine bar with a terrace overlooking the Moselle.
new.tip: Visit at golden hour and ask for a local Riesling.

new.title: Settle in at the Cochemer Weinstube on the Moselle promenade
new.desc: The Cochemer Weinstube is a wine tavern with restaurant on the Moselpromenade in Cochem, beside the river.
new.tip: Come for a glass of Moselle wine with a river view.

new.title: Taste wine at the Kloster Ebernach estate
new.desc: Weingut Kloster Ebernach in Cochem-Sehl is run by a family that leases the traditional estate. The monastery itself was founded in 1130 as a priory of Laach and now belongs to the Alexian brothers.
new.tip: Book a tasting with the winery before you go.

new.title: Tour the Vulkan Brauerei and its basalt beer cellar
new.desc: The Vulkan Brauerei in Mendig was founded in 1875 as the Wölker brewery and is the only one left of the 28 breweries that once stored beer in the basalt quarry caves. Guided tours cover the glass brewery, the cellars and a tasting.
new.tip: Book a tour ahead and bring a jacket for the cold cellars.

new.title: Rest in the Hofgarten courtyard of the Meyer-Näkel estate
new.desc: The Hofgarten Gutsschenke of the Meyer-Näkel estate in Dernau is a leafy courtyard inn serving wine and good food.
new.tip: A good stop on the Rotweinwanderweg. Check opening days.

new.title: Join a vineyard walk and tasting at Meyer-Näkel
new.desc: The Weingut Meyer-Näkel at Friedensstraße 15 in Dernau is a highly awarded Ahr red wine estate that offers a two-hour guided vineyard walk with a tasting afterwards.
new.tip: Book the walk in advance.

new.title: Taste Ahr Spätburgunder at Weingut Kriechel
new.desc: Weingut Kriechel on Walporzheimer Straße is the largest private family estate in the Ahr valley, with about 20 hectares of vineyards around Ahrweiler, Walporzheim and Bad Neuenahr, and offers tastings and tours.
new.tip: Ask for the red Spätburgunder and book a group tasting in advance.

new.title: Taste steep-slope Riesling at Heymann-Löwenstein in Winningen
new.desc: Weingut Heymann-Löwenstein in Winningen goes back to a family roots from 1520, and Reinhard Löwenstein founded the modern estate in 1980. It now covers about 15 hectares of Riesling vineyards with sites such as Uhlen.
new.tip: Book a tasting in advance.

new.title: Visit the Knebel family estate in Winningen
new.desc: Weingut Reinhard und Beate Knebel in Winningen is a family estate with roots back to 1642 that makes almost entirely Riesling from the steep Winningen slopes, including the Uhlen and Röttgen sites.
new.tip: Visits are by appointment, so book in advance.

new.title: Dine at Altdeutsche Weinstube Zum Lamm in Oberwesel
new.desc: The Altdeutsche Weinstube Zum Lamm in Oberwesel offers wines and traditional cuisine in a cozy dining room in the town centre.
new.tip: Go in the evening and check opening days first.

new.title: Find the tiny Weinstube Zum Toni above Oberwesel
new.desc: Weinstube Zum Toni in Engehöll opened in 2011 and is a very small wine bar with about 25 seats, open on weekends.
new.tip: Check the weekend opening hours before you go.
new.q: Weinstube Zum Toni, Am Kapellenberg 10, Oberwesel

new.title: Taste Middle Rhine wine in the Schönburg castle wine room
new.desc: The Schönburger Weinstube is a wine room in Burg Schönburg above Oberwesel, part of the castle hotel and open to outside visitors as well as hotel guests.
new.tip: Reserve a table and plan time for the castle walk.

new.title: Sip Riesling at Stephans Weinstube in Beilstein
new.desc: Stephans Weinstube in Beilstein is a small wine bar overlooking the Moselle with a sunny terrace. The owner is also the winemaker and often advises guests in person. Tarte flambée and cakes are on offer.
new.tip: Check the opening days and ask the owner about the wine.

new.title: Have cake and coffee at Café Kesseler in Bad Ems
new.desc: Café Kesseler on the Römerstraße in Bad Ems is praised by reviewers for its cakes and breakfast.
new.tip: Go for breakfast or an afternoon cake break after the Kurhaus.

new.title: Lunch with a view at the Burgrestaurant Lahneck
new.desc: The Burgrestaurant at Burg Lahneck has an outdoor terrace looking over the Rhine and Lahn.
new.tip: Check the seasonal opening times and combine with a castle tour.

new.title: Dine inside Rheinfels castle
new.desc: Some outer buildings of Burg Rheinfels now serve as a hotel, wellness centre and restaurant above the Rhine.
new.tip: Reserve ahead and combine with a castle tour.
